## What it is

Gelman's post compares the standing of computer science today with that of economics in the early 2000s and of Freudian psychiatry in the 1950s: each at the "apex academic and social prestige and influence" of its time. Economists used to be "the country's all-purpose pundits"; now "there's a new hegemonic science in town, and it's information science, or computer science." Computer scientists, he grants, have "earned it through all the amazing things they've built."

The phrase comes in a parenthesis about who now speaks with that authority: "Nowadays, many computer scientists and tech lords present themselves, and are often taken as, all-purpose pundits. (Many of the tech lords are actually tech investors; they've absorbed the prestige of information science through the transitive property of money.)" The prestige flows from the science to the people who fund it, and from there to whatever they choose to talk about. Gelman's worry is the familiar one: "you get the same problem we had before, which is when the gurus and their hangers-on start to believe their own hype."

## Why it matters

Prestige is supposed to track expertise, and expertise is specific to a field. When an audience treats money, or closeness to a prestigious field, as a sign of general authority, the people who get heard on a question are not the people who know most about it. Gelman also notes a pattern in how this ends: "It's when a group is at its most overvalued that it wants even more", and economists stopped asking for more influence once they became "just one more group."

## How it works

Gelman's post makes a sociological observation and has no model. Here is a toy version, our own. Each would-be pundit has some expertise on a given topic and some wealth. An audience decides whom to listen to by a mix of the two: credibility = expertise + $w$ × wealth, plus noise. With $w = 0$, attention goes to expertise. As $w$ grows, prestige passes from money to the speaker, whatever the topic.

## Simulated example

On a topic outside technology, 100 domain experts and 100 tech investors offer opinions. The experts know more about the topic; the investors have more money. The audience listens to the 20 voices it finds most credible.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {rng, range, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof w = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "Weight the audience gives to wealth (w)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 155, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
pundits = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const people = range(200).map(i => {
    const investor = i >= 100;
    const expertise = investor ? r.normal(-1, 1) : r.normal(1, 1);   // on this topic, sd units
    const wealth = investor ? r.normal(2, 0.7) : r.normal(0, 0.7);   // log scale, sd units
    return {who: investor ? "Tech investor" : "Domain expert", expertise, wealth, cred: expertise + w * wealth + r.normal(0, 0.5)};
  });
  const cut = people.map(d => d.cred).sort((a, b) => b - a)[19];
  const rated = people.map(d => ({...d, heard: d.cred >= cut}));
  const heard = rated.filter(d => d.heard);
  const mostExpert = people.slice().sort((a, b) => b.expertise - a.expertise).slice(0, 20);
  return {rated, investorsHeard: heard.filter(d => d.who === "Tech investor").length,
          expHeard: mean(heard.map(d => d.expertise)), expBest: mean(mostExpert.map(d => d.expertise))};
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  ariaLabel: "The transitive property of money: simulation chart",
  ariaDescription: "Horizontal axis: wealth (log scale, standard deviations). Vertical axis: expertise on the topic (standard deviations). Color shows domain experts and tech investors; filled dots are the 20 voices the audience listens to. The chart updates with the controls above it, and the summary below the charts states the result in words.",
  height: 300,
  x: {label: "Wealth (log scale, sd units)", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Expertise on the topic (sd units)", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Domain expert", "Tech investor"], range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(pundits.rated.filter(d => !d.heard), {x: "wealth", y: "expertise", stroke: "who", r: 3}),
    Plot.dot(pundits.rated.filter(d => d.heard), {x: "wealth", y: "expertise", fill: "who", r: 5})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`With wealth weighted at **${fmt(w, 2)}**, **${pundits.investorsHeard}** of the 20 most-heard voices on this topic are tech investors. Those 20 voices have an average expertise on the topic of **${fmt(pundits.expHeard, 2)}**, against **${fmt(pundits.expBest, 2)}** for the 20 people who actually know the most. ${w === 0 ? "With no weight on money, attention follows expertise." : "The money passes its prestige on to the speaker, whatever the topic."}`}</div>`
```

## R {.unlisted}

```{.r}
# The transitive property of money: wealth buys a hearing on any topic.
w <- 1 # weight the audience gives to wealth # <1>
set.seed(155) # <2>

investor <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), each = 100)
expertise <- ifelse(investor, rnorm(200, -1, 1), rnorm(200, 1, 1)) # <3>
wealth <- ifelse(investor, rnorm(200, 2, 0.7), rnorm(200, 0, 0.7))
cred <- expertise + w * wealth + rnorm(200, 0, 0.5) # <4>
heard <- rank(-cred) <= 20 # the 20 most-heard voices # <5>
best <- rank(-expertise) <= 20 # the 20 who know most
cat(sum(heard & investor), " of the 20 most-heard voices are tech ",
  "investors\nAverage expertise: most heard ",
  round(mean(expertise[heard]), 2), ", most expert ",
  round(mean(expertise[best]), 2), "\n",
  sep = ""
)

plot(expertise, cred, # <6>
  pch = ifelse(heard, 19, 1),
  col = ifelse(investor, "#d6604d", "#2166ac"),
  xlab = "Expertise on the topic", ylab = "Credibility with audience"
)
legend("topleft", c("Domain expert", "Tech investor", "Filled: most heard"),
  col = c("#2166ac", "#d6604d", "black"), pch = c(19, 19, 19),
  bty = "n"
)
```
1. The page's control: how much weight the audience gives to wealth.
2. Fixes the random numbers so the run is reproducible.
3. On this topic the domain experts know more and the tech investors know less.
4. Credibility with the audience: expertise plus w times wealth. The money's prestige passes to the speaker.
5. The 20 voices that get heard.
6. Credibility against expertise, the most-heard voices filled. With w above zero, the investors are heard on a topic they know least about.

## Python {.unlisted}

```{.python}
# The transitive property of money: wealth buys a hearing on any topic.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

w = 1  # weight the audience gives to wealth
rng = np.random.default_rng(155)

investor = np.repeat([False, True], 100)
expertise = np.where(investor, rng.normal(-1, 1, 200),
                     rng.normal(1, 1, 200))
wealth = np.where(investor, rng.normal(2, 0.7, 200), rng.normal(0, 0.7, 200))
cred = expertise + w * wealth + rng.normal(0, 0.5, 200)
heard = np.argsort(-cred).argsort() < 20       # the 20 most-heard voices
best = np.argsort(-expertise).argsort() < 20   # the 20 who know most
print(f"{np.sum(heard & investor)} of the 20 most-heard voices are tech "
      "investors")
print(f"Average expertise: most heard {expertise[heard].mean():.2f}, "
      f"most expert {expertise[best].mean():.2f}")

for g, c, name in [(~investor, "#2166ac", "Domain expert"),
                   (investor, "#d6604d", "Tech investor")]:
    plt.scatter(expertise[g & ~heard], cred[g & ~heard], facecolors="none",
                edgecolors=c)
    plt.scatter(expertise[g & heard], cred[g & heard], color=c,
                label=f"{name} (filled: most heard)")
plt.xlabel("Expertise on the topic")
plt.ylabel("Credibility with audience")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Prestige earned by a field (computer science) passes to the people who fund it, and from them to whatever they talk about.
- Gelman sees the same pattern as economics in the early 2000s and Freudian psychiatry in the 1950s: a field at its peak, whose gurus become all-purpose pundits.
- Expertise is specific to a field. Money and association are not evidence of knowing about the topic at hand.
:::
